difference) / 2 and the larger is (sum + difference) / 2.","The unit-attached phrasing '$10 more than' is sufficient to select the additive branch over the multiplicative branch in price contexts."]},"claim":"The pen costs $1.25, derived from the covering principle that an additive difference relation N = P + 10 composes with a sum N + P = 12.50 to force P = (S - D) / 2.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'costs $10 more than' were intended as a multiplicative relation (e.g., '10 times as much'), the additive elimination would not apply and P would instead be 12.50 / 11 \u2248 1.136.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the sum constraint were not over the same currency unit or excluded tax while the difference included it, the two constraints would not be jointly linear over a common unit and P = 1.25 would not follow.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the problem allowed negative prices or partial credits, alternative boundary readings could survive, but under standard non-negative price semantics P = 1.25 is uniquely determined.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Let the pen cost P and the notebook cost N. The problem supplies two simultaneous linear constraints over the reals: (1) N + P = 12.50 (sum), and (2) N = P + 10 (additive difference). Substituting (2) into (1) gives (P + 10) + P = 12.50, so 2P = 2.50, hence P = 1.25. The covering principle is: whenever two quantities have a fixed sum S and a fixed additive difference D (larger minus smaller), the smaller quantity is (S - D) / 2. This is the canonical two-equation/two-unknown elimination, and it is privileged here because the unit-attached '$10' in 'costs $10 more than' forces an additive rather than multiplicative reading.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
